summary: Sean Hollister recaps day one of the Epic v. Google jury trial over whether Google Play makes Android an unlawful monopoly. He argues Epic's opening painted a simple good-versus-evil story, while Google spent its time explaining complicated business practices. Evidence on both sides, including Epic's Project Liberty and Google's auto-deleted chats, may shape the jury's view.
one_line: On day one of Epic v. Google, Epic's simple bully-versus-underdog narrative seemed to land better with the jury than Google's complicated business explanations.
key_facts: Epic sued Google in 2020 after a fight over in-app purchase fees, claiming Google Play makes Android an unlawful monopoly.
Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein called Google a bully and a cheat that "bribes" or "blocks" attempts to compete with Google Play.
Epic says Google earns 70 percent profit margins on $12 billion in annual app revenue.

Bornstein cited an alleged $360 million payment to Activision to keep it from opening a competing app store; Activision told The Verge in 2022 it "never entered into an agreement that Activision would not open its own app store."
Epic's attorney admitted Google "was too clever" to draw up contracts that specifically forced developers not to compete with the Play Store.
Google's opening statement lasted 45 minutes; lead attorney Glenn Pomerantz argued Google and Apple compete against each other because phone quality can't be separated from app store quality.
Pomerantz noted every Samsung phone comes with two app stores on the homescreen, so Play's dominance reflects user choice.

Pomerantz said over a billion people have gone through the process of getting apps outside the Play Store; Google clarified this means users who enabled the Android sideloading flow, not necessarily completed installs.

Google highlighted Epic's secret "Project Liberty," a plan to update Fortnite to bypass app store fees, get kicked off Apple's and Google's stores, and sue, but Epic mentioned it first in its own opening.
Google employees, up to and including CEO Sundar Pichai, set sensitive chats to auto-delete, and the court has already decided Google should be sanctioned in some way.
Bornstein said of the destroyed chats: "as bad as the documents are, is worse. Or at least it was worse, before they were destroyed."
The first two witnesses were Epic Games Store head Steve Allison and Yoga Buddhi CEO Benjamin Simon, who also appeared in the Epic v. Apple trial.
Epic hinted that Google's 70/30 revenue split may rest on an arbitrary decision Valve made two decades ago with Steam.
